match.reason: No point in the bank covers differentiation or positioning; the closest, on competitors and market research, are related ideas rather than the same one, so this needs a new point.

draft.title: Differentiation and positioning
card: making a product stand out from competitors in a way buyers notice. It might be through quality, design, service or features.
the place a product holds in customers' minds compared with rivals. A business may aim to be seen as the cheapest, the most luxurious or the most reliable.
Differentiation is something the business does to the product. Positioning is the image that forms in the minds of customers as a result.
A business gives a clear message about its position, for example through its advertising and its price. If customers do not see the difference, the product is hard to tell apart from its rivals.
draft.remember: Differentiation sets a product apart. Positioning is where customers place it against rivals.

a.q: Which example shows positioning rather than differentiation?
opts: Customers see a brand of tyres as the most reliable
A tyre maker adds a longer warranty to its range
A tyre maker designs a new tread pattern for wet roads
A tyre maker offers free fitting at its own stores
a.why: Positioning is how customers see a product compared with rivals, so seeing the tyres as the most reliable is a position. The other three are actions the business takes to make its product stand out, so they are differentiation.
a.clue: Positioning happens in the minds of customers.

b.q: Nina opens a bakery in Orange. Her bread looks and tastes like her rivals' bread. She spends heavily on advertising that says it is the most luxurious in town. What is the likely problem?
opts: Customers may not see a real difference behind the claim
Positioning only works for businesses selling cheap goods
Advertising cannot change how customers see a product
The bakery has differentiated but has not tried to position
b.why: Nina is trying to claim a position, but her bread is no different from her rivals', so customers may not believe it. Positioning can be luxury as well as cheapest, and she has not differentiated her product, so the message may fail.
b.clue: Ask whether customers have a reason to believe the message.

a.best: Customers see a brand of tyres as the most reliable

b.best: Customers may not see a real difference behind the claim

b.q: Nina opens a bakery in Orange. Her bread looks and tastes like her rivals' bread. She spends heavily on advertising that says it is the most luxurious in town. What is the likely problem?
opts: Her bread has no real difference to back up her claim
She has differentiated her bread but not positioned it
Her advertising gives customers no message about position
Her bread is too different from her rivals' to compare
b.why: Nina is claiming a luxury position, but her bread is the same as her rivals', so customers have no reason to believe it. It is tempting to say she has differentiated but not positioned, but it is the other way round: her advertising tries to position the bread, and she has done nothing to make it stand out.
b.clue: Ask whether customers have a reason to believe the message.

problems.detail: Saying positioning is just 'the image that forms in the minds of customers as a result' of differentiation oversimplifies. In HSC Business Studies, positioning is also a deliberate strategy the business chooses and communicates, not only a by-product of changing the product.

'Differentiation is something the business does to the product' clashes with the card's own example of service, which is not a change to the product itself. 'A business gives a clear message about its position' reads as if every business always does this; it should say 'aims to give' or 'should give'.

The card never says that a claimed position needs a real difference to back it up. It only says the business sends a message through advertising and price, which Nina does. The right answer leans on the clue and the why rather than on anything the card teaches.

The right option is the only one that starts with 'Customers' rather than 'A tyre maker', and the clue says positioning happens 'in the minds of customers'. A student can match the words without understanding the idea.
